explanations.explanation: Tarshish it is, friend. Jonah says that's where he was so quick to flee (Jonah 4:2). He says it right in his prayer to the LORD, which takes some nerve.

Egypt is a good guess, friend, but Jonah never says it. In his prayer he says he was so quick to flee toward Tarshish (Jonah 4:2). I know how it feels to end up somewhere you didn't plan, but I never picked the drawer. Jonah picked his own direction.
Damascus is a real city, friend, but it's not in Jonah's prayer. He says he was so quick to flee toward Tarshish (Jonah 4:2). I'd have asked somebody for directions, and I'd have been lost anyway.

explanations.answer: God is gracious and relents from disaster
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Jonah says he knew God is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, One who relents from sending disaster (Jonah 4:2). So the reason he gives for running is who God is. He says it right out loud to the LORD, and honestly, I love him for the honesty.

explanations.answer: The Ninevites would never listen to him
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. Jonah never says that, and the Ninevites did listen. God saw them turn from their evil ways (Jonah 3:10). What Jonah says he knew was that God is gracious and relents from sending disaster (Jonah 4:2). His whole problem was that the news was too good.

explanations.answer: The journey there was too long and dangerous
explanations.explanation: Nice try, friend, but the text doesn't mention the road at all. Jonah says he knew God is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and One who relents from sending disaster (Jonah 4:2). That's his reason, in his own words. A long walk I could understand, but that isn't the reason Jonah gives.

Careful, friend, that's not what he asks. Jonah says, “…please take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live.” (Jonah 4:3). He asks for his own life to end, and nothing about Nineveh in that request. I think this one is heavy, so I'll just say the LORD answers him next (Jonah 4:4).

Right, baker, it's false. Jonah asks, “…please take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live.” (Jonah 4:3). He's not asking for Nineveh's destruction here. I think this is a heavy moment, and it's good to notice the LORD doesn't brush him off.

explanations.answer: Have you any right to be angry
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker, that's the question. “Have you any right to be angry?” (Jonah 4:4). Jonah asks to die and the LORD answers with a question, a short one. I wish I could answer my own grumpy days with a question like that.

explanations.answer: Do you not remember the great fish
explanations.explanation: It's a clever guess, friend, but that question isn't in the text. The LORD replies, “Have you any right to be angry?” (Jonah 4:4). One short question is all He says in that verse.

explanations.answer: Will you go back to your own country
explanations.explanation: That one isn't in the text, friend. The LORD simply asks, “Have you any right to be angry?” (Jonah 4:4). He doesn't send Jonah anywhere in that moment. He just asks and lets it sit there, which is harder than it sounds.

True, baker. Jonah leaves the city, makes a shelter, and sits in its shade to see what will happen to the city (Jonah 4:5). He's out there watching. I think he's still hoping for a different ending, but that part is my guess.

It's true, friend, though I see why it sounds odd. The text says Jonah made himself a shelter and sat in its shade to see what would happen to the city (Jonah 4:5). So he sat there on purpose, watching Nineveh. I'd have brought cookies, but that's me.

A vine, baker! The LORD God appointed a vine, and it grew up to provide shade over Jonah's head to ease his discomfort (Jonah 4:6). Jonah already had a shelter, and now he had a vine over his head too. That's shade with a bonus.
Close on the shade, friend, but it's not a fig tree. The text says the LORD God appointed a vine (Jonah 4:6). It grew up over Jonah's head to ease his discomfort. A plain old vine did the job.

Good memory for a Bible plant, friend, because a broom tree does shade someone in the Bible, Elijah the prophet in 1 Kings 19:4. But here the text says the LORD God appointed a vine (Jonah 4:6). Different story, different plant.
True, baker. The text says Jonah “…was greatly pleased with the plant.” (Jonah 4:6). A little shade will do that to a person. I've been pleased with less.

Not false, friend. Jonah “…was greatly pleased with the plant.” (Jonah 4:6). He was angry earlier in the chapter, and now he's delighted with a plant. I think a little shade can turn a lot of moods around.
A worm, baker. When dawn came the next day, God appointed a worm that attacked the plant so that it withered (Jonah 4:7). A worm took down the plant. I've lost a whole batch to less, believe me.

Locusts are a very Bible kind of answer, friend, but not here. The text says God appointed a worm that attacked the plant so that it withered (Jonah 4:7). One little worm was all it took. No swarm needed.

A goat would work fast on a vine, friend, I'll give you that. But the text says God appointed a worm that attacked the plant so that it withered (Jonah 4:7). The worm did the job, and no goat was needed.

Not this time, friend. With the sun beating down, Jonah grows faint and wishes to die, saying, “…it is better for me to die than to live.” (Jonah 4:8). He doesn't say the LORD was right. I think the heat made him feel worse, and that's my guess, not the text's.

Right, baker, it's false. Jonah grows faint and says, “…it is better for me to die than to live.” (Jonah 4:8). There's no admission about Nineveh here. The sun was beating on his head, and what he says is about himself, not Nineveh.

explanations.answer: He is angry enough to die
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Jonah says, “I do… I am angry enough to die!” (Jonah 4:9). He doesn't back down an inch. I'll say it plainly: when a man is arguing with God over a vine, someone is in a tough spot.

explanations.answer: He is sorry he got so angry
explanations.explanation: That would have been a nice turn, friend, but it's not what happens. Jonah answers, “I do… I am angry enough to die!” (Jonah 4:9). He doesn't say sorry. He holds his ground, even when the ground is a withered vine.

explanations.answer: He has no right to be angry
explanations.explanation: Jonah says the opposite, friend. When God asks if he has any right to be angry about the plant, he replies, “I do… I am angry enough to die!” (Jonah 4:9). He's sure he's right. I think that's what makes the LORD's next words land so hard.

explanations.answer: Should He not care about the city of Nineveh
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The LORD asks, “So should I not care about the great city of Nineveh…” (Jonah 4:11). Jonah cared about a plant he didn't make, so the LORD points to a city full of people. It's a question, and the LORD leaves it there.

explanations.answer: Why did Jonah never thank Him for the plant
explanations.explanation: Good thought, friend, but the LORD doesn't ask about thanks. He says Jonah cared about the plant he neither tended nor made grow (Jonah 4:10). Then He asks, “So should I not care about the great city of Nineveh…” (Jonah 4:11). The question turns from the vine to the city.

explanations.answer: Will Jonah go back into the city to preach
explanations.explanation: That isn't the question, friend. Jonah already preached there (Jonah 3:4). The LORD asks, “So should I not care about the great city of Nineveh…” (Jonah 4:11). He's talking about His care, not Jonah's next trip.

True, baker. The LORD says Nineveh has more than 120,000 people “…and many cattle as well?” (Jonah 4:11). He names the cattle right after the people. I'll admit, I didn't expect the cows to make it into the last verse.

It's true, friend, and I get why it sounds funny. The LORD says Nineveh has more than 120,000 people “…and many cattle as well?” (Jonah 4:11). The cattle are right there at the end of the verse. They made the final line of the book.
